planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Phoenix continues setting fruit through the high daytime and nighttime temperatures of a Gulf South summer that cause blossom drop in most other tomato varieties.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or cage for support; consistent watering reduces blossom end rot in humid conditions. Phoenix is a tomato variety developed by the Texas A&M AgriLife vegetable breeding program specifically to keep setting fruit through the extreme heat of a Texas and Gulf South summer, when night temperatures above 75°F cause pollen sterility and blossom drop in most standard varieties. The medium-sized, firm, deep red globe fruits also carry useful resistance to common soilborne diseases and cracking, and the vines continue producing through the hottest stretch of summer that typically causes a production gap in southern tomato gardens. It also carries a degree of protection against sunscald thanks to good foliage cover. A dependable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners who want tomatoes to keep coming through July and August rather than stalling out, in zone 4–11.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Program
Texas A&M AgriLife Research — Vegetable Breeding

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+); soak seed overnight to speed germination. Stewart's Zeebest is a tall, vigorous Louisiana heirloom that continues producing tender pods over a long, hot Gulf South summer.

directions: Sow directly into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest pods every 1–2 days at 3–4 inches, since this tall, heavy-yielding variety puts on pods quickly in summer heat and older pods turn woody fast. Stewart's Zeebest is a Louisiana heirloom okra, grown for generations by home gardeners in the Gulf South for its tall, vigorous plants and heavy, extended production of smooth, tender, dark green pods with excellent flavor and relatively low fiber even at a slightly larger picking size than typical spineless varieties. The tall habit (commonly 6–8 feet by late summer) makes it useful as a seasonal privacy screen or windbreak in the vegetable garden in addition to its culinary value, and the plants shrug off the heat and humidity that stress many garden crops in July and August. A reliable, long-producing regional heirloom for Gulf South okra lovers, zone 5–11.

common_name: Golden Bush Scallop Squash (Golden Custard Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 65°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the compact bush habit needs less room than vining squash but still benefits from generous spacing for airflow and easy harvest.

directions: Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest fruit young, at 2–3 inches across, for the sweetest, most tender flesh and thinnest skin, and pick every couple of days to keep the compact bush producing all summer. Golden Bush Scallop is a classic American heirloom summer squash producing the traditional flying-saucer-shaped 'patty pan' fruit in a bright, buttery golden-yellow, with a scalloped edge and creamy, mild, slightly nutty flesh when harvested young. The compact, non-vining bush habit keeps the plant tidy and productive in a relatively small footprint compared to sprawling vine squash, making it a good choice for smaller vegetable gardens and raised beds. Like all summer squash, frequent harvest at a small size is the key to extended production — fruit left to grow large quickly turns tough and seedy and signals the plant to slow down. A cheerful, productive, old-fashioned squash for zone 3–11 gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F, in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the very short 6-week maturity makes this an excellent choice for succession planting through the whole Gulf South growing season, from spring through a final late-summer sowing.

directions: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and one of the fastest-maturing Southern peas available, ready to pick as fresh shell peas in as little as six weeks. Six Weeks Purple Hull is a classic, widely grown heirloom cowpea prized above all for its speed — the compact, semi-bush plants set pods and fill out quickly, making it the go-to variety for gardeners who want an early first picking or need to squeeze in extra succession plantings between other summer crops. The pods mature to a deep purple that makes ripe pods easy to spot against the green foliage, and the cream-colored peas inside have the classic mild, earthy purple hull flavor, excellent fresh-shelled and cooked down Southern-style with a bit of pork or simmered as a simple pot of field peas. Reliable, heat-tolerant, and fast, it is a Gulf South garden staple for a quick, dependable pea crop, zone 5–11.

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F, in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; give the vigorous vining plants a trellis, fence, or plenty of ground to sprawl, and expect a long production season lasting until frost.

directions: Direct sow in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, thriving with minimal irrigation through the hottest, driest part of the Gulf South summer. Red Ripper is a vigorous, long-vining heirloom cowpea grown across the South since the 19th century both as a food crop and as a dependable summer cover crop and livestock forage, valued for its toughness in poor soil and drought that would fail most other legumes. The sprawling vines carry deep red-brown, kidney-shaped seeds in long pods over an extended late-summer season, continuing to set new pods until the first frost, which makes it one of the longer-producing Southern peas for a continuous late-season harvest. Beyond the table, Red Ripper is prized as a nitrogen-fixing green manure and grazing forage crop, tilled or turned under at the end of the season to build soil fertility for the following year. A dual-purpose, low-input heirloom well suited to the toughest garden conditions, zone 5–11.
